extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, and serious inquirers into method and scientific investigation
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for discovering sciences and correcting errors of the understanding: how to observe, experiment, define, and reason so as to avoid the various 'idols' and fallacies that corrupt philosophy and natural inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance observation of differences and resemblances
rubrics_metrics.description: Some minds are more vigorous in observing differences, others in observing resemblances; each tends to excess (catching at niceties or shadows of resemblance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interchange modes of contemplation so the understanding is both penetrating and capacious; avoid dwelling exclusively on fine distinctions or only on broad analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject factions of ancients versus moderns
rubrics_metrics.description: Some evince unbounded admiration for antiquity, others embrace novelty; both extremes are prejudicial to sciences and produce partisan judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth is found in nature and experience, not in the authority of any particular age; avoid allowing party zeal for ancients or moderns to determine assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate contemplation of particulars and generals
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemplation of individual forms distracts and weakens; contemplation of general composition stupefies and relaxes the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interchange and employ both particular and general contemplation in turn to render the understanding both penetrating and wide, preventing the idols arising from each extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ward off and expel the idols of the den
rubrics_metrics.description: Idols of the den (private cave) arise from predominant pursuits, excess in synthesis/analysis, party zeal, or the extent/narrowness of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He who contemplates nature should suspect whatever particularly fixes his understanding and exercise caution to preserve an equable and unprejudiced mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware idols of the market (words and names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words react upon the understanding; associations of words and names entwine and make philosophy sophistical and inactive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed carefully in disputes about words by defining terms (as mathematicians do), but ultimately rely on particular instances and their regular series and arrangement to ground notions and axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of word-imposed idols: fictitious names and confused abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Words impose idols either as names of non-existent things (fictions) or as names of actual objects but confusedly and hastily abstracted from things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fictional names can be removed by refutation or disuse; confused abstractions are deeper and require careful analysis and return to particulars to clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for degrees of distortion in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words are less faulty (names of substances, esp. less abstract species), actions are more faulty, and qualities (except immediate objects of sense) are most faulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially cautious with abstract qualities (e.g., heavy, light, rare) and seek more determinate notions grounded in sense and instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject idols of the theatre (dogmatic theoretical systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Idols of the theatre are instilled by the fictions of theories and depraved rules of demonstration; they impose sectarian systems and distort inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt wholesale confutation of every sect here; rather note that theatrical systems often found philosophy on too narrow grounds and drag experiment to suit pre-established decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize three sources of false philosophy: sophistic, empiric, superstitious
rubrics_metrics.description: False philosophies arise from (1) sophistic/logical corruption (e.g., Aristotle's logical excesses), (2) empiric reliance on a few experiments (alchemists), and (3) superstition/theological mixing (Pythagorean, Platonist tendencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of each: sophistic over-generalizes by logic, empiricists generalize prematurely from few cases, superstitious systems mix divine/textual authority with natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid founding philosophy on too narrow or too scanty experimental bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretic philosophers who take too much from a few topics or too little from many found their systems on too scanty grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend inquiry beyond isolated experiments; neither rely on a handful of examples nor on broad meditation without reduction to verified experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer investigation of active (operative) principles over stationary principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemplation of stationary principles (that from which things are) rather than active processes (by which things are created) is less useful; practice depends on active causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on active, operative qualities (attraction, repulsion, attenuation, etc.) and their roles in changes, since these yield practical knowledge and better penetrate nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pursue extremes (atoms or shapeless matter) at expense of useful intermediate objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract dissection to potential and shapeless matter or atoms penetrates little that is useful to advance human estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate on intermediate, practical objects and processes which afford means of action rather than metaphysical extremes that offer little utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intemperance of systems: hasty dogmatism and unbounded scepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Two excesses: those who decide hastily and make sciences positive and dictatorial; and those who propagate scepticism and unbounded inquiry, which enervates understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject both extremes: provide assistance to the senses and understanding without dogmatic closure or paralyzing infinite doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct the fourfold errors in the process from senses to axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: The process from senses and things to axioms contains four errors: (1) impressions of the senses are erroneous; (2) notions are improperly abstracted and confused; (3) induction employed is improper (simple enumeration); (4) the usual top-down method (general-first) generates error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address each: correct sensory defects, refine abstractions, reform induction beyond mere enumeration (include exclusions/resolutions), and adopt a better order of discovery than establishing the most general propositions first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience is the best demonstration if experiments adhere to what was actually made
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience is by far the best demonstration, provided it adhere to the experiment actually made; transferring experiments to other subjects blindly is fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blind transfer of experimental results; treat experiments as demonstrations only when methodical caution justifies their extension to similar subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments to elicit causes and true axioms (seek light over profit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many experiments are made carelessly or in sport; true course is to seek experiments which afford light (causes and axioms) rather than immediate profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate divine order: first assign whole effort to discover causes/axioms; prefer experiments that illuminate principles which prepare abundant practice, rather than seeking quick practical gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend experiments broadly rather than isolating solitary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobody can successfully investigate the nature of any object by considering that object alone; inquiry must be generally extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wasting time on solitary probes; vary and extend experiments to new effects and wider contexts to reveal general causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge philosophies by their fruits (practical outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all signs none is more certain than that of the fruits produced; systems that yield little useful experiment or assistance to mankind are futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account that which is unproductive or produces only dispute (thistles and thorns) is to be deemed futile; value systems that produce practical, improving results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess systems by their growth and progress (systems founded on nature will increase)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those founded on nature grow and increase; those founded on opinion change not. Mechanical arts (founded on experience) continually improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer methods and systems that show continuous improvement and productive advancement rather than stationary, unproductive doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat authors' confessions and unanimity/dissension as diagnostic signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Confessions by authorities about the subtilty of nature, widespread dissension among philosophers, or superficial unanimity (often due to prejudice) are signs of weakness in systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such external signs (origin, age, fruits, progress, authors' confessions, dissension, and dubious unanimity) to gauge the soundness of philosophical systems; unanimity is often a bad augury and dissension indicates the path from senses to understanding is not well prepared.
